titles.l4: What fractions can do that whole numbers cannot
titles.l6: Why fractions can divide and integers cannot
titles.l7: Division, and the system that supports it

kernelIdea: ℚ is closed under addition, additive inverses, multiplication, and multiplicative inverses of nonzero elements — this makes it a field.

kernels.l1: Half a cookie is a real amount. Pieces are numbers too.
kernels.l2: When sharing does not come out whole, the answer is a piece of a whole. Once pieces are allowed, every sharing has an answer — except sharing among nobody.
kernels.l3: Adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing fractions always gives another fraction, as long as you never divide by zero. The reciprocal is exactly what the whole numbers were missing.
kernels.l4: Add, subtract, multiply or divide two fractions — dividing by anything but zero — and the answer is a fraction again. That last one is what the integers could not do, and it is the whole reason fractions were built.
kernels.l5: The fractions obey every arithmetic rule the integers do, and add one more: every nonzero one has a reciprocal. That extra property is exactly what the integers were missing.
kernels.l6: The fractions are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by anything nonzero. The integers fail that last one, having no reciprocals, and every closure proof here is fraction arithmetic checked against the definition.
kernels.l7: The fractions are closed under all four operations, with division defined whenever the denominator is nonzero. The proofs are the standard fraction formulas, read as closure statements.
kernels.l8: ℚ is the field of fractions of ℤ, the smallest field containing it; finite fields ℤ/pℤ show that fields need not be infinite, and characteristic distinguishes them.
